Dr. Rafiqul Rahman with Mr. Tufail Ur Rahman with Mr. Serajur Rahman, Ms. Sufia Ahmed Mr. A.K.M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury Mr. Hasnat Quiyaum, Advocates ----- for the Appellants
Dr. Kamal Hossain with Mr. Ramzan Ali Sikder Mr. A.Q.M. Shahidul Islam Advocates ----- for the Respondents
parties:
Bangladesh Power Development Board and others
Vs.
M/s. Builders Corporations

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that the plaintiff was given the contract for erection of a Suspension and Anchor Tower on the right bank of Labukhali River crossing (Barisal side) by work order dated 25.4.1990, followed by conclusion of a formal agreement for the purpose. It was stipulated between the parties that the drawing and design of the Tower shall be supplied by the defendant Board and the Contractor will erect the Tower in pursuance of the said drawing and design. It was further stipulated that the defendant Board shall supply all materials for the construction of the Tower and the plaintiff contractor shall complete the construction of the tower within 180 days with the materials supplied by the Board. It was also agreed between the parties that the plaintiff contractor shall execute the work of the project under the supervision of the engineers of the Board. The height of the Tower was fixed at 527 feet and the weight of the Tower stood at 181.07 tonnes. The plaintiff contractor after completing the foundation work of the Tower erected Section 14 (first section) attached to the foundation of the Tower under the supervision of the officers of the defendant. On successful completion of the first section of the Tower, the contractor started erection of Section 13 of the Tower under the supervision of the engineers of the defendant. Subsequently the plaintiff completed erection of Section 12 of the Tower and started erecting Section 11. It has been alleged that during all these days the defendant made no grievance regarding the quality of the work done by the plaintiff contractor. Unfortunately on the night following 15.1.1993 the Tower collapsed at Section 11. A team of officers of the board investigated the matter and the team found that Tower allegedly collapsed due to loose joints of nuts and bolts. It was alleged that the plaintiff did not adapt the correct method of tower erection consequent upon which the Tower collapsed. It was further contended that the security money and performance guarantee of the plaintiff was illegally withheld. It has been alleged by the plaintiff that the Tower collapsed due to defect of drawing and design and not due to any fault of the plaintiff contractor. After the collapse of the tower, the plaintiff contacted the defendant for further instructions in the matter but in vain. In the meantime, the staff of the plaintiff remained idle at the works cite for quite a considerable period involving huge expenditures for the plaintiff contractor. Eventually the defendant illegally terminated the contract and hence the suit for damages. 

 4. Subsequently the plaintiff contractor served a notice upon the Chairman of the Board on 1.10.1994 requesting him to appoint an arbitrator to resolve the dispute between the parties within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice but the latter did not respond. Thereafter, the plaintiff was constrained to apply to the Court for appointment of an arbitrator. The learned Subordinate Judge and Arbitration Court started Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1995 under section 8 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and appointed Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator. On a reference from the Court the learned arbitrator assumed jurisdiction of the case and notified the parties to appear before him with necessary papers in support of their respective claims within the specified time. The plaintiff contractor duly filed statement of claims before arbitrator and the defendant Board filed its objection denying all the material allegations of the plaint and asserted that the claims of the plaintiff were false and frivolous. It was specifically contended that there was no defect in the drawing and design of the Tower in question and the material supplied to the plaintiff contractor for the erection of the Tower were perfectly good. It was clearly asserted that due to the loose fittings of the nuts and bolts and application of incorrect method for the implementation of the Project and due to poor workmanship the Tower collapsed, causing heavy loss and injury to the PDB. The defendant also seriously contested the competence of the learned arbitrator to resolve the dispute between the parties. This objection regarding jurisdiction and authority of the arbitrator was duly noted by the learned arbitrator and a specific issue was framed on it. The learned arbitrator without answering this issue in accordance with law by passed it on the ground that since he was appointed arbitrator by the Court, he would not entertain any objection regarding his jurisdiction to act as the arbitrator. 

 5. The plaintiff contractor examined one witness before the learned arbitrator, who supported the plaintiffs case and proved a series of documents while the defendant Board also examined one witness and produced a series of documents in support of its case. 

 9. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant appellant, submits that in the face of clear stipulation in Clause G.C. 12 of the Contract, Director, Distribution and Inspection (II/III) PDB, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka is to be the sole arbitrator in case of any dispute between the parties but the plaintiff contractor never approached the designated arbitrator to resolve the dispute and consequently the arbitration Court had no authority to appoint Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator in this case, beyond the contemplation of the parties. Dr. Rahman submits that in view of the specific and unequivocal stipulation in the contract it is the designated officer who alone was to be the sole arbitrator in any dispute between the parties, thereby leaving no scope for arbitration by any other person, the specified and designated arbitrator having never been .approached by the plaintiff contractor, Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury had no authority to assume jurisdiction as the sole arbitrator and to enter upon the reference and consequently all actions taken and things done by him must be held to be void ability and of no legal consequences. Dr. Rahman argues that the designated arbitrator having never been called upon to arbitrate the dispute, the learned arbitration Court had no authority to appoint Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator in this case in terms of section 8(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and consequently the disputed award filed by the learned arbitrator in the Court of the learned arbitration Court is evidently illegal and without jurisdiction and consequently of no legal effect. The learned Counsel further submits that in view of the admitted fact that the arbitration proceeding was not completed within the stipulated period of 4 months, the arbitrator had no legal authority to extend the time for the arbitration proceeding without the order of the Court. The learned Counsel further submits that the learned arbitrator committed a clear illegality in not mentioning in the award the fees and other charges, which he had received from the plaintiff contractor, which is a requirement of law under section 14 of the Arbitration Act and thereby misconducted himself The learned Counsel also submits that the leaned Arbitrator also misconducted the proceedings by appointing a practicing Advocate as the Secretary to the Arbitrator, never disclosing his function and his remuneration and the party or parties who paid same, and this novel procedure inevitably raised serious suspicion regarding an unfair deal in the whole proceeding. The learned Counsel further submits that the total price of the contract of the project being Taka 51,37,683/75, the learned Arbitrator awarded Taka 80,11,500/- alone as salary and wages of the staff of the plaintiff contractor as mentioned in Item Nos. VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, and XII of the schedule of the plaint without at all considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record and this renders the award one-sided and totally unacceptable to reason and prudence. The learned Counsel argues that in view of the fact that which the total value of the work of the Project stands at Tk. 51,37,683.75 only, awarding an award for Tk. 5,31,11070.75 only as loss and damages to the contractor is not only unconscionable and fantastically exorbitant but also it betrays a total lack of application of a reasonable mind on the part of the learned Arbitrator as well as the learned arbitration Court, totally ignoring the facts of the case and the material evidence on record and as such the impugned judgment and decree making the award the Rule of the Court must be set aside in the interest of justice. 

 11. Dr. Kamal further submits that in view of the fact that the learned Arbitrator assumed jurisdiction on the order of the Court and the defendant Board never raised any objection regarding his assumption of jurisdiction as the sole arbitration and willingly took part in the arbitration proceedings, the appellants plea of want of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator is no longer available to the appellant. Dr. Kamal strenuously argus that necessary security for the award having not been furnished, the case is barred under article 154 of the Limitation Act and as such this appeal is clearly not maintainable in law. 

 14. The learned Counsel for the appellant has placed before us the statement of claims of the plaintiff contractor, reply thereto by the defendant Board, the arbitration award dated 19.3.2001 made by Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, the evidence of the 2 witnesses examined by the learned Arbitrator (though deposition of DW.1 does not contain any signature of the learned Arbitrator) and the exhibited documents. From a reading of Clause G.C. 12 of the agreement, which forms the basis of the case, it is clearly found that in case of any dispute between the parties over the work of the Project in question the matter requires to be referred to a designated arbitrator, namely the Director, Distribution and Inspection (PDB), Motijheel Commercial area, Dhaka. In the face of this clear and unambiguous stipulation in the contract itself, it was incumbent upon he plaintiff contractor to approach the designated arbitrator to resolve the dispute but without doing so, the contractor wrote a letter to the Chairman of the defendant Board for appointing an arbitrator for the purpose. This letter was obviously an unwanted and futile exercise of power and, consequently the Chairman of the Board had every reason to ignore it in the light of stipulation of the agreement itself. This obviously did not absolve the plaintiff contractor of his obligation to call the specifically designated Engineer of the defendant Board to act as the sole arbitrator in the case in terms of the agreement itself. Instead, the plaintiff went to the Arbitration Court in hot haste without taking necessary steps in the matter as envisaged by Clause G.C. (12) of the agreement. 

 15. From a reading of section 8(1). of the Arbitration Act, 1940 it becomes clear that the Court can appoint an Arbitration when approached by a party after the contending parties failed to reach a consensus on the appointment of the sole Arbitrator. In our present case, we do not find any scope for application of section 8(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940. Obviously the learned Arbitration Court acted illegally in appointing Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator in fragment violation of Clause G.C. (12) of the agreement which provides for arbitration by a Designated Engineer of the Board. The learned Subordinate Judge and Arbitration Court had evidently no authority to act under section 8 of the Arbitration Act to appoint the sole arbitrator in total disregard of the clear and unambiguous provision made in the arbitration agreement. In the facts of the case and the materials on record it must be found that Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury assumed jurisdiction as the sole arbitrator in the case illegally and arbitrarily. The question of jurisdiction of Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury to act as the sole arbitrator was raised by the contesting defendant at the earliest opportunity, which is evident from the arbitration ward itself, wherein a specific issue was raised by the learned Arbitrator regarding maintainability of the arbitration proceedings before him. It is unfortunate that without going through and considering the arbitration clause G.C. 12 of the agreement, the learned arbitrator illegally assumed jurisdiction and entered upon the arbitration reference on the plea that since the Court appointed him as the sole arbitrator, no objection would be entertained by him on this score. The question of jurisdiction was also raised by the appellant before the learned Joint District Judge and the Arbitration Court. It is unfortunate that the learned Arbitrator as well as the learned arbitrator Court treated the question of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator in a most casual fashion, being completely oblivion of the provision of Clause G.C.12 of the agreement and coerced the defendant Board to accede to the authority of the Arbitrator. We are, therefore, satisfied that the principle of waiver estoppel and acquiescence shall not stand against the defendant Board in raising the question of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator, which cuts at the root of the case. Since the arbitrator initially lacked jurisdiction, act as the sole arbitrator in the case beyond the agreed stipulation of the parties, this inherent deficiency cannot be bridged up by subsequent developments, dispute consistent objection of the defendant Board. We find support of this view in the case of Inter Trade Ltd. Vs. Trading Corporation of Pakistan Ltd., reported in PLD 1976 (Karachi) 496 in which it has been held that the power of the Court under section 8 of the Arbitration Act does not confer the authority on the Court to substitute the original agreement of the parties by entirely a new agreement of its own choice in defence to the contemplation in the agreement between the parties that a dispute arising in the future shall have to be referred to the designated arbitrator. 

 16. Regarding the submission of Dr. Rafiqur Rahman that the learned arbitrator misconduct himself in not mentioning in the award the amount of fees and other charges he had received and from whom he had so received as required by section 14 of the Arbitration Act merits consideration. As a matter of fact, at no point of time the learned Arbitrator divulged these material facts and kept these as guarded secrets for unknown reasons. The question of remuneration of the secretary to the arbitration also remains an undisclosed fact. The learned Arbitrators overzealously is clearly manifested from the fact that he indulged in extra-ordinary lengthy cross-examination of the witnesses covering over 15 pages, thereby assuming the role of a prosecutor than that of an arbiter. Award of Taka 81,50,000/00 as salary of the staff of the contractor for a work worth Taka 51,13,768/00 only, is evidently unusual and unacceptable to reason and prudence. It is equally preposterous and unconscionable to award Tk. 5,31,11070.75 to the plaintiff contractor for a deal fixed at 51.13, 768.00, only without assigning any acceptable reason whatsoever. The learned Arbitrator practically accepted the contractor’s claims as a matter of course. We, therefore, find sufficient substance in the submissions made by the learned Cousel for the appellant. 

 17. Dr. Kamal Hossain has referred to us the case of Swarm Kumar; Roy and others vs. Sukamal Chandra Roy and others, reported in 6 DLR 477, the case of Messers R. Sim Co. Vs. Messers Pak. Industries Jute Mills, reported in 8 DLR-305, the case of Md. Mujibar Rahman Sar-Vs- The Deputy Commissioner, Pabna, reported in 1984 BCR (AD) 353 and the case of the Chief Engineer, Building Department Provincial, Government of Sind-Vs-Messers Pak, National Construction Company, Reported in PLD 1981 (Karachi) 553, the Case of Subal Chandra Kundu-Vs-The State of West Bengal, reported in AIR. 1952 (Cal) 235, and the case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by Director, Movement and Storage Department of Food-Vs-Jalal Uddin Ahmed, reported in 36 DLR (AD) 27 in support of his contentions. Dr. Kamal's submission that after the parties consented to extension of time for completing arbitration beyond four months merits consideration and it prevails. 

 18. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, on the other hand, has referred to us the case of Ms. M. M. Ispahani Ltd.-Vs-M/s. Pakistan Trading Company reported in 16 DLR 260 and the case of Hasmat Ali Jamadar and others-Vs-Asmatali Jamadar and others, reported in 6 DLR 478 in support of his contention. 

 19. We have carefully gone through the cited decisions. The ratio dividend of the above-noted citations is not in dispute. We find that the facts and circumstances of the present case being clearly distinguishable from those of the cited cases, the decisions referred to above by Dr. Kamal do not help the respondent contractor in any way. 

 20. On the other hand, the decisions cited by the learned Counsel for the appellant apply in full force in the present case. We, therefore, find substance in the submission of Dr. Rafiqur Rahman and these are accordingly sustained. 

 21. After giving our anxious considerations to the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, we are constrained to find that the learned arbitration Court acted illegally and without jurisdiction in appointing Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator in this case in terms of section 8 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and consequently all actions taken and things done by Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury must be found illegal and without jurisdiction as being coram non judice. The disputed award is, therefore, not an award in the eye of law. The learned Joint District Judge and Arbitration Court was manifestly wrong in ignoring the clear provision of arbitration agreement and illegally made the disputed award the Rule of the Court without properly applying his judicial mind into the facts of the case and the materials on record. Consequently, we find substance in the appeal. The appeal succeeds.
